summary: Defines MIB objects for managing pseudowire encapsulation of structured or unstructured TDM circuits, such as T1, E1, T3 and E3, across packet switched networks.

eli5.summary: Old phone lines send their signals in a fixed steady rhythm. This provides gauges for watching those lines when they are carried over a modern packet network.

subtitle: The SNMP objects used to configure and monitor T1, E1, T3 and E3 circuits carried as pseudowires over a packet network.

tldr.problem: Operators who carry TDM circuits such as T1, E1, T3 and E3 across a packet switched network need a standard way to configure those emulated circuits and to watch how they behave.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5604 defines the PW-TDM-MIB module. It adds a TDM table, a table of shared configuration parameters and three performance tables (current, 15-minute intervals and daily intervals) on top of the generic pseudowire MIB.
tldr.outcome: A manager can set up a TDM pseudowire through SNMP and track lost packets, jitter buffer problems and error seconds. It is a Proposed Standard and no newer RFC replaces it.

today: RFC 5604 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the MIB Manages
sections.content:
RFC 5604 describes a model for managing TDM pseudowires: TDM data encapsulated for transmission over a Packet Switched Network (PSN). Here TDM means the Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy (PDH). The module can describe TDM signals in Structure Agnostic Transport mode (E1, T1, E3 and T3) or in Structure Aware Transport mode (E1, T1 and NxDS0), as defined in RFC 4197.

The MIB is closely related to the documents that define the encapsulations themselves: SAToP, TDMoIP and CESoPSN. A TDM connection is a pseudowire connection. It is not treated as an interface, so it does not appear in the ifTable.
sections.eli5: Some old phone-style lines get squeezed into packets so they can travel over a computer network. This document lists the settings and counters a manager needs to run them.

sections.title: Where the Module Fits in the Layers
sections.content:
The TDM management model has several MIB modules, following the layering in the PWE3 architecture of RFC 3985. The TDM PW MIB sits in the service layer. It works with the DS1, DS3 and DS0 MIBs for the circuit itself, the generic pseudowire MIBs below it, the MPLS VC MIBs and the MPLS MIBs at the bottom.

The module is designed to fit that architecture, support edge-to-edge emulation of any TDM connection, configure the connection, and report alarms, counters and status objects. Connection-specific behavior comes from supplementary MIB modules such as those for TDMoIP and CESoPSN.

The RFC also fixes the vocabulary for direction. PSN-bound traffic is TDM data received, packetized and sent into the PSN. CE-bound traffic arrives from the PSN and is reassembled through a jitter buffer before play out to the TDM line. The size of that buffer SHOULD be locally configurable to absorb packet delay variation.
sections.eli5: Think of a stack of floors in a building. The TDM floor is the top one, and it talks to the generic pseudowire floor below it, which talks to the network floors at the bottom.

sections.title: Tables and Pseudowire Types
sections.content:
The MIB has five tables:

  • pwTDMTable holds generic TDM information about the pseudowire: the ifIndex of the TDM interface, an index into the generic configuration table, an index into a specific configuration table, config error bits and status values.
  • pwTDMCfgTable holds generic configurable parameters for any TDM type.
  • pwTDMPerfCurrentTable holds statistics for the current 15-minute period.
  • pwTDMPerfIntervalTable holds historical 15-minute intervals, usually 96 entries to cover 24 hours.
  • pwTDMPerf1DayIntervalTable holds daily intervals, usually 30 entries to cover a month.

The agent creates a pwTDMTable entry for every pwTable entry whose pwType is between 17 and 24. The TDM interface can be a full link such as an E1 or DS3, or the interface of a bundle holding the time slots to be sent. Many pseudowires of the same kind can share one configuration entry.

The object pwTDMRate gives the bit rate in multiples of 64 kbit/s. For structure-agnostic E1 it is 32, for E3 it is 535 and for T3 it is 699. T1 uses 24 in basic mode and 25 in the octet-aligned mode. For structure-aware emulation it is the number of DS0 channels.
sections.eli5: There is one main list of lines, one list of shared settings, and three scoreboards: one for right now, one for each quarter hour and one for each day.

sections.title: Setting Up a TDM Pseudowire
sections.content:
Configuration follows a fixed order. First configure the interface layer using the DS1-MIB and/or DS3-MIB. If it applies, create a bundle of time slots with the DS0 Bundle MIB. Then create an entry in the generic pwTable and configure the PSN tunnels as the PW MIB (RFC 5601) describes. Finally, create entries in pwTDMCfgTable and, if needed, in the specific table, and set their indices in pwTDMTable. After setup, check that no error bits are set in pwTDMConfigError.

The RFC gives two worked examples. The first is a DS1 connection: pwTDMCfgPayloadSize is 43 payload bytes, packet reordering is off, no RTP header is used and the jitter buffer depth is 30000 microseconds. The second is a pseudowire of 3 DS0 time slots, built over a bundle and the TDMoIP MIB, with pwType set to 24.

pwTDMConfigError has bits that flag a mismatch with the peer: tdmTypeIncompatible, peerRtpIncompatible and peerPayloadSizeIncompatible.
sections.eli5: You build the line in steps, like assembling a toy: the wire first, then the pipe, then the settings. At the end you look at a warning light to see if anything does not match the other side.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
The generic configuration table collects the knobs that shape a TDM pseudowire.

  • pwTDMCfgPayloadSize is the payload size in bytes. A received packet that does not fit that size MUST be treated as malformed when the length field is 0.
  • pwTDMCfgPktReorder turns on re-ordering of out-of-order packets inside the jitter buffer. Some implementations may not support it, and then the agent should reject a SET to true.
  • pwTDMCfgRtpHdrUsed says whether an RTP header is prepended. The default is false.
  • pwTDMCfgJtrBfrDepth sets the jitter buffer depth in microseconds. The default is 3000.
  • pwTDMCfgPktReplacePolicy chooses what is played out when packets are missing: all ones (the default, which plays AIS), an implementation-specific pattern, or a user-defined filler byte from pwTDMCfgPktFiller.
  • pwTDMCfgTimestampMode chooses absolute or differential timestamps. All implementations that support the RTP header MUST support absolute mode.

Other objects set the thresholds for the loss-of-packet-state (LOPS) logic. pwTDMCfgConsecPktsInSynch (default 2) counts consecutive in-sequence packets needed to leave LOPS. pwTDMCfgConsecMissPktsOutSynch (default 10) counts consecutive missing packets needed to enter it. The alarm threshold defaults to 2500 ms and the clear-alarm threshold to 10000 ms. Most of these objects may be changed only while the pseudowire is not active.
sections.eli5: These are the dials on the control panel. Some say how big each parcel is, some say how long to wait for late parcels, and some say what to play if a parcel never shows up.

sections.title: Performance Counters and Intervals
sections.content:
The performance tables use the same set of counters in each. They count missing packets (found through gaps in the control word sequence number), packets reordered, jitter buffer underruns, out-of-order packets that were dropped and malformed packets. They also count Error Seconds (ES), Severely Error Seconds (SES), Unavailable Seconds (UAS) and failure counts (FC).

Any malformed packet, sequence error or LOPS counts as an error second. A second becomes a severely errored second when the percent of missing packets in a 1-second window reaches pwTDMCfgMissingPktsToSes, which defaults to 30. Any consecutive ten seconds of SES are counted as one unavailable second. A failure event begins when LOPS is declared and ends when it clears.

After 15 minutes the current entry is copied into the interval table and reset to zero. An agent keeps up to 96 intervals of 15 minutes; the minimum is 4 and the default is 32. Daily intervals range up to 30. Counters keep collecting while the interface is down. They use the PerfCurrentCount and PerfIntervalCount textual conventions, which are Gauge32 because the values can decrease.
sections.eli5: Every quarter hour the scoreboard is saved to a notebook and wiped clean. Later you can flip back through the notebook to see when the line had trouble.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module has read-write and read-create objects, and setting them without protection can hurt network operations. Unauthorized access to pwTDMTable and pwTDMCfgTable could disrupt traffic on the network. The readable tables also reveal TDM pseudowire connectivity topology and performance, so administrators may treat them as sensitive.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC says SNMPv3 VACM and USM MUST be used with any SNMPv3 agent that implements the module, recommends the SNMPv3 cryptographic features, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The control panel can break the lines if the wrong person pushes buttons, so it needs a good lock. Only the right people should be allowed to look or touch.
